claims.text: The untreated eutectic HEA has a hierarchical dual-phase FCC/B2 lamellar microstructure.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
Dislocation accumulation or pile-ups near internal lamellar interfaces produce local stress concentrations, microcracks, and premature failure.
Cryogenic rolling followed by annealing can produce a refined hierarchical microstructure in a lamellar eutectic HEA.
Cryogenic rolling introduces a high density of heterogeneous dislocation structures.
Cryogenic rolling refines the lamellar spacing.
Low-temperature annealing causes partial recrystallization while preserving a heterogeneous mixture of fine and coarse or unrecrystallized regions.
Differences in strain partitioning between constituent phases generate differing recrystallization driving forces.
The treatment creates nano- to submicron-scale structural domains.
The treated microstructure has a broad or graded distribution of local hardness.
The network of fine interfaces redistributes and arrests dislocation motion.
The heterogeneous microstructure reduces dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries.
The heterogeneous microstructure enhances back-stress strengthening.
Reduced pile-ups and distributed back stresses delay crack nucleation and propagation.
Cryogenic rolling and annealing increase elongation to failure relative to the as-cast alloy.
Cryogenic rolling and annealing retain or increase yield and ultimate tensile strength relative to the as-cast alloy.
Excessive recovery or recrystallization during annealing can coarsen or eliminate the beneficial hierarchical lamellar structure.
The claimed benefit applies under room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing.

contradictions.description: The intervention is called a 'single-step' route, but it explicitly contains two sequential processing operations: cryogenic rolling and subsequent annealing. It can reasonably be treated as one integrated intervention, but not literally as one processing step.
